text: Lessons eighty and eighty-one covered physical streaming replication, a byte-for-byte copy of an entire cluster. This lesson covers PostgreSQL's other replication mechanism — logical replication, which works at the row and table level using a publish and subscribe model.

On the source database, a publication names a set of tables whose row-level changes get made available for replication. On the destination, a subscription connects to that publication and applies incoming changes — but the subscriber's tables have to already exist with a matching structure first, since logical replication moves data into existing tables, it doesn't create schema for you.

Because a publication names specific tables instead of the entire cluster, you can replicate just a few tables to a downstream database. And because it replicates decoded row changes instead of raw WAL, the subscriber doesn't need to match the publisher's PostgreSQL major version — which is exactly why this becomes a migration strategy in Lesson 84. What it doesn't give you is automatic DDL replication or a simple promotable failover target.

Choose logical replication for selective or cross-version data movement, physical replication when you need a complete failover target. Next up: connection pooling with PgBouncer, and why PostgreSQL's process-per-connection model makes pooling matter more than in thread-based engines.
